case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbour Reach Logistics (HRL) is a private limited company in the container freight and port logistics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2007 by Alan Truscott, it moves imported goods for national retailers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. HRL plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated container-handling crane system, financed by an $800,000 ten-year bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $320,000 a year, a variable cost of $24 a unit and a selling price of $32, and currently produces 60,000 units a year, each unit a billable container consignment. HRL faces a growing skills gap: 18 of its 50 drivers and crane operators are not certified on the new automated system, and defect complaints at the terminal are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The container terminal handled 15,000 consignments last quarter at a damage defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average truck turnaround time is 4.5 hours. A survey of 500 freight clients found that 68% would pay a 3% premium for guaranteed two-day delivery, and 57% rate on-time reliability as their top criterion. A skills audit shows 18 of 50 staff are not certified on the new automated crane; external certification courses cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbour Reach Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on HRL's $800,000 variable-rate bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.00 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026, increasing the wage bill for its 50-strong workforce. (3) Diesel fuel prices have risen 9.0% year-on-year and port handling charges are up 4.0%, while demand for container freight grew 2.5%.

questions.question_text: HRL financed part of its $1,200,000 automated crane investment with an $800,000 bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HRL of using retained profit rather than the bank loan for this expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $400,000 carries no interest charges or capital repayments, so it protects HRL's cash flow while the business already services an $800,000 bank loan and carries fixed costs of $320,000 a year. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on the new automated container-handling crane without raising the $32 selling price, helping HRL win the 68% of surveyed freight clients who would pay a premium for reliable two-day delivery.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with founder Alan Truscott and avoids the collateral conditions attached to the $800,000 loan, so the $1,200,000 expansion cannot be repossessed if freight demand disappoints. It also lets HRL act quickly on the skills gap among 18 uncertified staff by funding training from internal funds rather than seeking further bank approval, protecting the contribution earned on each of 60,000 container consignments and leaving the loan available for future working capital.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HRL, its financing mix and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: HRL is promoting its guaranteed two-day container delivery service. Consider national trade-journal advertising, social media marketing, or direct sales calls to freight clients. Which should HRL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-journal advertising: A campaign in freight and logistics journals would reach many retail supply managers at once and build HRL's reputation as a reliable container carrier, supporting the premium two-day service. However, a full-page national campaign is expensive for a 50-employee firm already funding an $800,000 loan, and much of the readership lies outside the coastal catchment HRL actually serves, so a large share of the spend is wasted.

Social media marketing: Targeted posts and short videos of the new automated crane can reach prospects cheaply and be measured through clicks and enquiries. The 57% of surveyed clients who rank on-time reliability first can be shown the falling defect complaints directly. The drawback is that freight buyers are often procurement managers who rely on trade contacts, so engagement may be weak relative to the 15,000 consignments HRL must fill each quarter.

Direct sales calls to freight clients: A sales team can call the 500 surveyed clients and national retailers individually, demonstrate the two-day offer and negotiate the 3% premium that 68% said they would accept. This builds on existing relationships, gives immediate feedback on the 26 monthly complaints and targets the highest-volume accounts. It is slower to build broad awareness than print and uses staff time, but conversion per contact is high and it directly fills the 60,000-unit capacity.

Recommendation: HRL should choose direct sales calls as its main method, supported by low-cost social media. Direct calls turn the finding that 68% of 500 clients would pay a 3% premium into real bookings and handle complaints personally, which a journal campaign cannot do. Trade-journal advertising is rejected as too costly and untargeted for a 50-staff company servicing a loan; social media alone is rejected because its audience is too diffuse for specialist container freight.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to HRL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HRL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of HRL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade-journal advertising and social media alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: HRL's autocratic leadership and the 18 uncertified staff are contributing to a skills gap and rising defect complaints. Explain two benefits for HRL of adopting a democratic leadership style to improve motivation and commitment in its terminal team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 50 drivers and crane operators to share ideas about how the new automated crane is run, which addresses the skills gap and raises motivation through involvement and recognition of their experience. When staff help design shift routines and safety checks, they are more likely to attend and to apply the training they receive, directly reducing the defect complaints at the terminal.

Point 2: Consulting the workforce builds commitment to the $1,200,000 investment and lowers the risk of resistance to new working methods under the previous autocratic style. Because 18 staff are not yet certified, their input helps target the $750 certification courses where they are most needed, raising productivity toward the 1,200 units per worker implied by 60,000 units and 50 staff, and protecting the contribution earned on every consignment handled for national retailers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HRL's leadership change, certification problem and output.

questions.question_text: HRL must train 18 staff to operate the new automated container-handling crane. Consider on-the-job training or external certification courses at $750 per employee. Which should HRL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the terminal on the actual automated crane is directly relevant to HRL's own equipment and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 15,000 consignments handled each quarter and the effort to cut the 2.2% defect rate. Its weaknesses are that trainer-operators have their own work interrupted, bad habits can spread, and there is no recognised certificate, which may not satisfy the 57% of clients who rate reliability highly when they audit HRL.

External certification courses at $750 per employee: These give structured, up-to-date skills and a formal qualification for all 18 uncertified staff (18 × $750 = $13,500), a sum that is small against the $1,200,000 expansion. They remove staff from the crane during the course, reducing short-term capacity, and the generic content may not match HRL's exact crane settings, so some on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: HRL should choose a sequence that starts with on-the-job training and then adds external certification for the 18 staff, funded from the $1,200,000 budget. On-the-job training comes first because it is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids losing capacity while the skills gap is urgent; certification-only is rejected because paying $13,500 and taking 18 people off the crane at once would disrupt the two-day delivery promise to the 68% of clients who value it, and certificates can be added once operations stabilise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HRL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of HRL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of HRL with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HRL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $320,000 ÷ ($32 − $24) = $320,000 ÷ $8 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $32 − $24 = $8. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HRL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HRL can compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 60,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 20,000 units, to judge whether the $1,200,000 automated crane is justified.
2. Contribution of $8 per unit lets managers model a discount: a cut of $2 in the $32 price would leave $6 contribution, still covering the $320,000 fixed costs at 60,000 units, so a price promotion can be tested safely.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $320,000 and contribution of $8 helps set the volume needed to service the $800,000 bank loan before committing more capital.
4. Labour productivity of 60,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,200 units per worker can be benchmarked each quarter to assess whether the 18 certified staff and falling defect complaints are improving efficiency.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 60,000-unit output; discount modelling on the $32 price; loan-service volume for the $800,000 debt; and productivity benchmarking at 1,200 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HRL's profitability using the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HRL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $2,000,000 to $2,500,000 while cost of sales moved from $1,200,000 to $1,375,000; gross profit therefore increased from $800,000 to $1,125,000. Dividing gross profit by revenue gives 40.0% in 2024 and 45.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $250,000 on revenue of $2,000,000 and $375,000 on $2,500,000 produces 12.5% and 15.0%. Operating profit measured against capital employed of $1,250,000 and $1,500,000 gives 20.0% and 25.0%.

Evaluation: All three margins improved, so profitability strengthened. The rise in gross profit margin from 40.0% to 45.0% shows HRL kept more of each revenue dollar after direct container-handling costs even as volume grew, helped by the $8 contribution on each consignment. The operating margin rising from 12.5% to 15.0% indicates fixed costs of $320,000 were absorbed more effectively. Returns on the larger capital base improved from 20.0% to 25.0%, suggesting the $1,200,000 crane investment is already earning. However, interest payable rose from $30,000 to $40,000 as the $800,000 loan bites, and the 57% of clients demanding reliability means any service failure could quickly reverse these gains.

Conclusion: HRL's financial performance has clearly improved: gross margin, operating margin and returns on capital all rose together, and the gains are not merely a revenue effect. The main risk is the rising interest burden, so HRL should protect the improved margins by using retained profit to reduce borrowing while demand for container freight remains strong.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether HRL's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HRL of introducing the guaranteed two-day delivery premium promoted in its market research.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The research found that 68% of 500 freight clients would pay a 3% premium for guaranteed two-day delivery, so introducing it can raise revenue per consignment and protect the $8 contribution as diesel costs rise. It also appeals to the 57% of clients who rank on-time reliability first, strengthening HRL's position with national retailers and supporting the case for the $1,200,000 automated crane that makes the promise achievable.

Disadvantage: A guaranteed two-day promise raises operating risk: the terminal's average 4.5-hour truck turnaround and 2.2% defect rate mean any delay causes missed deadlines and compensation claims, potentially undoing the fall in complaints from 44 to 26 per month. Keeping the guarantee may also require extra resources that push up the $320,000 fixed costs or the $24 variable cost per unit, squeezing the margin if not all clients accept the 3% premium.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HRL's research data, service reliability and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.0% rise in diesel fuel costs will affect HRL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If HRL's $800,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the rise adds 0.75 percentage points (5.00% − 4.25%), so the extra annual interest is 0.75% × $800,000 = $6,000 a year. That is modest beside fixed costs of $320,000 a year, and if the loan were fixed-rate the direct cost would be zero. Higher base rates may still deter retailers from premium freight and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but HRL can largely neutralise this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 per hour): With a workforce of 50, most terminal and driving roles are hourly-paid, so this rise feeds straight into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so no honest annual wage total can be invented; the defensible comparison is with given productivity of 60,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,200 units per worker. If productivity holds, a wage rise is affordable; if it slips, unit labour cost rises and the $8 contribution per consignment is squeezed.

Diesel fuel rise (9.0%) and port charges (4.0%): These hit HRL's $24 variable cost on every one of the 60,000 consignments. The insert does not decompose variable cost, so only an illustrative bound can be shown: if all $24 were fuel and it rose 9.0%, that would be 9.0% × $24 = $2.16 per unit, or about $129,600 a year at 60,000 units — but fuel is only part of the cost, so the real figure is lower and cannot be quantified from the insert. The impact is nonetheless widespread and hard to pass on when only 68% of clients accept a premium.

Conclusion: The 9.0% diesel rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across every consignment, cannot be removed by simply fixing a rate as interest can, and is harder to offset than the wage rise because productivity is already only 1,200 units per worker. The interest rise is the smallest at $6,000 a year, and the wage increase is significant but manageable if productivity holds; fuel touches the $24 variable cost that underpins the whole $8 contribution.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HRL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HRL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HRL with a well-justified judgment that diesel fuel inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
